newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Further Ireland, Finland gains limited.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Further Ireland, Finland gains limited.

text.p: Irish and Finnish bonds offer little prospect of further gains on convergence now their inclusion in the first wave of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) has been largely priced in, analysts said on Friday.
But entry to EMU is not a foregone conclusion, with features other than the Maastricht criteria weighing negatively on their chances, they said.
"All the positive convergence between those markets and the core markets has already taken place," said Stephen King, chief European economist at HSBC James Capel in London.
"The market has discounted that both Ireland and Finland could be in the first wave of EMU."
At 1330 GMT, the Finnish benchmark bond due 2006 was yielding 46 basis points over 10-year Bunds compared with 42 basis points at the beginning of 1997.
The Irish/German 10-year spread was at 89 basis points, in slightly from 92 at the start of the year.

Kirit Shah, chief strategist at Sanwa International in London, agreed that from a fundamental perspective both Ireland and Finland had a better chance of meeting the EMU criteria than countries like Italy and Spain.
But both King and Shah said other factors would also play a part in the decision over EMU entry.
"If it is the politicians who decide who is in or out of EMU, the fact that a country has made the criteria is perhaps a little less relevant than the size of the economy," said Shah.
He said both markets are seen as small and illiquid and because of that, fund managers do not give them much attention.

The fate of Ireland and Finland regarding EMU could not be considered without also looking at Italy and Spain. In terms of sentiment, Shah said that was important as a broad EMU could be difficult to sell to the German electorate.

"The moment you try to include Ireland and Finland because they have made the criteria, it will open a Pandora's box," he said. "If you allow these small countries in then you have to come to some agreement that bigger countries like Spain and Italy will be joining at a later date."
Analysts said the political, economic and geographical groupings of Ireland and Finland were also important factors.
"The links of the real economy to bigger neighbouring countries could create shocks after monetary union," said Shah.
Britain must be taken into account when looking at Ireland, while for Finland, analysts said Sweden, Denmark, Norway and the former Soviet Union must be considered.

"There are certain issues which could leave small countries with a heavily dependent trade partner outside EMU rather exposed ... (and) not really able to respond easily to changes in competitiveness of the larger partner," said King.
Analysts said the volatility and recent strength of the Irish pound from the link to sterling could hamper Ireland's EMU prospects.

"There are worries that Ireland could be overheating and hence need a monetary tightening, so there could be some conflict there between exchange and interest rate needs," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London.
"While Ireland has a good chance of getting into EMU, they might decide to stay outside just right at the beginning."
In Finland too the strength of the economy could be problematic for bonds, offseting some of the benefits from the political commitment to joining EMU in the first round.
"As long as the economy remains strong, the market is going to see it as inflationary and any scope for narrowing the yield spread might be quite limited," said Stamenkovic.
